Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১) Which is not a lower GIT symptom?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Explanation: Lower gastrointestinal (GIT) symptoms originate from the small intestine, colon, rectum, or anus. Common lower GIT symptoms include altered bowel habits (diarrhea or constipation), hematochezia (passage of fresh blood per rectum), and excessive flatus (wind). Xerostomia refers to dry mouth caused by reduced salivary secretion or salivary gland dysfunction. It is an oral/upper digestive tract symptom, not a manifestation of lower GIT disease. Therefore, xerostomia is the correct exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Lower GIT symptoms: Altered bowel habit, hematochezia, tenesmus, diarrhea, constipation, abdominal distension, flatus.

  • Hematochezia: Fresh blood per rectum; commonly due to lower GIT bleeding.

  • Melena: Black tarry stool; usually indicates upper GIT bleeding.

  • Xerostomia: Dry mouth due to reduced salivary secretion (e.g., Sjögren syndrome, anticholinergic drugs, dehydration).

Exam Pearl: Xerostomia is an oral symptom, whereas altered bowel habit, hematochezia, and excessive wind are classic lower GIT symptoms.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২) Which may precipitate or aggravate angina?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Explanation: Thyroxine increases the basal metabolic rate, heart rate, myocardial contractility, and myocardial oxygen demand. In patients with underlying coronary artery disease (CAD), this increase in oxygen demand may precipitate or aggravate angina pectoris. For this reason, thyroxine should be started at low doses and titrated gradually in elderly patients and those with ischemic heart disease. Although some NSAIDs may increase long-term cardiovascular risk, they are not the classic drug that directly precipitates angina in standard examination questions.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thyroxine increases:

    • Heart rate

    • Myocardial contractility

    • Cardiac output

    • Myocardial oxygen consumption

  • Start low-dose thyroxine in patients with CAD or the elderly.

  • Excess thyroid hormone can cause angina, palpitations, and atrial fibrillation.

  • Untreated hyperthyroidism may worsen ischemic heart disease.

Exam Pearl: Thyroxine increases myocardial oxygen demand; therefore, it can precipitate or worsen angina in patients with coronary artery disease.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩) Which is an autosomal recessive disease?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Explanation: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. The defect impairs hepatic copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin and biliary copper excretion, leading to progressive copper accumulation in the liver, brain, cornea, and other tissues. Clinically, it may present with hepatic disease, neurological or psychiatric manifestations, and Kayser–Fleischer rings. Myotonic dystrophy is autosomal dominant, as are both neurofibromatosis and Huntington disease. Autosomal recessive disorders typically require pathogenic variants in both alleles, with unaffected carrier parents potentially transmitting the disease to their offspring.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Wilson disease → Autosomal recessive → ATP7B

  • Copper accumulation → liver + basal ganglia + cornea

  • Kayser–Fleischer ring → characteristic of Wilson disease

  • Myotonic dystrophy → Autosomal dominant

  • Neurofibromatosis → Autosomal dominant

  • Huntington disease → Autosomal dominant

Exam Pearl: Wilson disease is a classic autosomal recessive disorder; remember “Wilson = AR.”

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪) Which is a bacterial disease?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Tetanus is a bacterial disease caused by Clostridium tetani, a Gram-positive, anaerobic, spore-forming bacillus. The organism usually enters the body through contaminated wounds and produces tetanospasmin, a neurotoxin that blocks inhibitory neurotransmission by preventing the release of GABA and glycine. This causes characteristic muscle rigidity and painful spasms, including trismus (lockjaw). Rabies is caused by a rabies virus, polio by poliovirus, and malaria by the protozoan parasite Plasmodium. Therefore, among the given options, tetanus is the only bacterial disease.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tetanus → Clostridium tetani

  • Tetanospasmin blocks GABA and glycine release

  • Classic feature → trismus (lockjaw)

  • Rabies → virus

  • Polio → poliovirus

  • Malaria → Plasmodium protozoa

Exam Pearl: Tetanus is a bacterial disease caused by Clostridium tetani.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫) Malar flush occurs in which valvular disease?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Explanation: Malar flush is a characteristic facial appearance classically associated with mitral stenosis (MS). It appears as a pink or reddish-purple flush over the cheeks, particularly in patients with significant or advanced mitral stenosis. The underlying mechanism is related to reduced cardiac output and peripheral vasoconstriction, together with pulmonary hypertension and altered blood flow. Mitral stenosis most commonly results from rheumatic heart disease and causes obstruction of blood flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle. MR, AS, and TR do not classically produce malar flush.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Malar flush → Mitral stenosis

  • MS → mid-diastolic murmur at the apex

  • Opening snap is characteristic of MS

  • Severe MS → pulmonary hypertension → right-sided heart failure

  • Malar flush is classically seen in advanced MS

Exam Pearl: Malar flush on the cheeks is a classic clinical clue to mitral stenosis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬) What will be the nature of pulse in LVF?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Pulsus alternans is a pulse characterized by alternating strong and weak arterial pulse waves despite a regular heart rhythm. It is classically associated with severe left ventricular failure (LVF) and reflects marked impairment of left ventricular contractility. The alternating stroke volume results from beat-to-beat changes in myocardial contractile force. Anacrotic pulse is classically associated with severe aortic stenosis, while pulsus bisferiens is associated with conditions such as combined aortic stenosis and regurgitation or hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy. Pulsus paradoxus refers to an exaggerated inspiratory fall in systolic blood pressure and is classically associated with cardiac tamponade and severe asthma/COPD.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • LV failure → Pulsus alternans

  • Pulsus alternans → alternating strong and weak pulse

  • Aortic stenosis → Anacrotic pulse

  • Aortic regurgitation → Collapsing/water-hammer pulse

  • Pulsus paradoxus → Cardiac tamponade

Exam Pearl: Pulsus alternans is a classic sign of severe left ventricular systolic failure.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭) Fine touch sensation is carried by fibre of which column?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Fine touch sensation is primarily carried by the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (DCML) pathway. First-order sensory neurons enter the spinal cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the posterior (dorsal) columns: the fasciculus gracilis carries information from the lower body, while the fasciculus cuneatus carries information from the upper body. These fibres synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei in the medulla, where second-order neurons decussate and ascend as the medial lemniscus. The posterior column pathway also carries vibration, conscious proprioception, and discriminative touch. Therefore, the posterior column is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fine/discriminative touch → Posterior column

  • Vibration → Posterior column

  • Conscious proprioception → Posterior column

  • Fasciculus gracilis → Lower limb

  • Fasciculus cuneatus → Upper limb

  • Pain and temperature → Anterolateral/spinothalamic tract

Exam Pearl: Fine touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception travel in the posterior column–medial lemniscus pathway.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮) What type of necrosis occurs in myocardial infarction?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Coagulative necrosis is the characteristic pattern of necrosis in myocardial infarction (MI). Ischemia causes irreversible cell injury and death, but the basic tissue architecture is preserved for several days because structural proteins and enzymes are denatured. Histologically, the infarcted myocardium develops coagulative necrosis, followed by an inflammatory response and subsequent replacement by granulation tissue and ultimately a fibrous scar. In contrast, liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain infarction and abscesses, caseous necrosis is classically associated with tuberculosis, and suppurative necrosis occurs in bacterial infections producing pus. Thus, coagulative necrosis is the classic answer for myocardial infarction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Myocardial infarction → Coagulative necrosis

  • Most solid-organ infarctions → Coagulative necrosis

  • Brain infarction → Liquefactive necrosis

  • Tuberculosis → Caseous necrosis

  • Abscess → Liquefactive/suppurative necrosis

Exam Pearl: Remember: MI = coagulative necrosis; brain infarction = liquefactive necrosis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯) Which one is a membranous organelle?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Peroxisomes are single-membrane-bound organelles containing oxidative enzymes such as oxidases and catalase. They are involved in very-long-chain fatty acid oxidation, detoxification of certain substances, and metabolism of hydrogen peroxide. In contrast, centrioles, ribosomes, and microtubules are non-membranous cellular structures. Ribosomes are composed of ribosomal RNA and proteins and are responsible for protein synthesis. Centrioles and microtubules are primarily composed of tubulin, with centrioles forming part of the centrosome and contributing to the organization of the cytoskeleton and mitotic spindle. Therefore, among the given options, peroxisome is the only membranous organelle.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Peroxisome → Single membrane

  • Peroxisome contains catalase

  • Major role → oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids

  • Ribosome → Non-membranous

  • Centriole → Non-membranous

  • Microtubule → Non-membranous

Exam Pearl: Peroxisome is a single-membrane-bound organelle; ribosomes, centrioles, and microtubules are non-membranous.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১০) Which is called double edged sword?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Metaplasia is called a “double-edged sword” because it is initially an adaptive, reversible response to chronic irritation or stress, but the altered tissue may lose normal protective functions and develop dysplasia and potentially malignancy if the stimulus persists. A classic example is squamous metaplasia of the respiratory epithelium in smokers. Although squamous epithelium is more resistant to irritation, it lacks the normal mucociliary clearance function and may increase the risk of subsequent neoplastic transformation. Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, and atrophy are also cellular adaptations, but the term “double-edged sword” is classically associated with metaplasia because of its protective benefit and potential pathological consequences.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Metaplasia → reversible adaptive change

  • Persistent stimulus → dysplasia → possible malignancy

  • Smoking → squamous metaplasia in respiratory epithelium

  • Barrett esophagus → intestinal metaplasia

  • Metaplasia itself is not cancer

Exam Pearl: Metaplasia protects against chronic stress but may predispose to dysplasia and malignancy — hence the “double-edged sword.”

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১১) Which neuroglia is mesodermal in origin?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Microglia are the resident immune cells of the central nervous system and are unique among neuroglia because they are derived from mesodermal/mesenchymal lineage rather than neuroectoderm. More specifically, microglia arise from yolk-sac macrophage precursors during early embryonic development. In contrast, astrocytes and oligodendrocytes are derived from neuroectoderm, particularly neural tube neuroepithelial cells. Ependymal cells also develop from the neuroectodermal neural tube lining. Microglia function as phagocytic and immune-surveillance cells in the CNS and become activated in response to infection, injury, and inflammation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Microglia → Mesodermal lineage

  • Microglia → CNS macrophages/phagocytes

  • Astrocytes → Neuroectoderm

  • Oligodendrocytes → Neuroectoderm

  • Ependymal cells → Neuroectoderm

  • Microglia originate from yolk-sac macrophage precursors

Exam Pearl: Microglia are the only major CNS glial cells derived from mesodermal lineage.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১২) Which is the first manifestation of almost all forms of injury to cells?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Cellular swelling is the earliest and most common manifestation of reversible cell injury. It results primarily from failure of ATP-dependent Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps, usually due to reduced oxidative phosphorylation and ATP depletion. Sodium accumulates intracellularly, followed by water, causing the cell and its organelles to swell. This change is also called hydropic change when more pronounced, with accumulation of water in the cytoplasm. Fatty change is more characteristic of injury to organs involved in lipid metabolism, particularly the liver, heart, and kidney, and is not the universal earliest response. Therefore, cellular swelling is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cellular swelling → earliest manifestation of cell injury

  • Usually indicates reversible cell injury

  • ATP depletion → Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure → Na⁺ and water accumulation

  • Hydropic change → more pronounced cellular swelling

  • Fatty change → particularly common in liver

Exam Pearl: The first morphological manifestation of most forms of cell injury is cellular swelling.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৩) What is the lining epithelium of tongue?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The tongue is covered predominantly by stratified squamous epithelium, which provides protection against mechanical trauma from chewing and swallowing. The dorsal surface has specialized mucosa containing papillae and taste buds, while the ventral surface is smoother and lined by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium. Much of the anterior dorsal tongue is covered by keratinized or parakeratinized stratified squamous epithelium, particularly over the filiform papillae, which are important for mechanical function. Therefore, among the given options, stratified squamous epithelium is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tongue → Stratified squamous epithelium

  • Ventral surface → mainly non-keratinized

  • Dorsal surface → specialized mucosa with papillae

  • Filiform papillae → keratinized, mechanical function

  • Fungiform, foliate, circumvallate papillae → associated with taste buds

Exam Pearl: The tongue is lined predominantly by stratified squamous epithelium.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৪) What type of metaplasia occurs in myositis ossificans?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Myositis ossificans is a form of connective tissue metaplasia in which mesenchymal cells within skeletal muscle differentiate into osteoblasts and chondroblasts, leading to formation of bone and cartilage in soft tissue. It commonly develops after trauma, particularly in muscles subjected to repeated injury. This represents heterotopic ossification rather than a true neoplastic process. Squamous and columnar metaplasia are epithelial adaptations and are therefore not applicable. “Tumor metaplasia” is not a recognized standard category of metaplasia. Thus, among the given options, connective tissue metaplasia is the best and accepted answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Myositis ossificans → Connective tissue metaplasia

  • Often follows trauma

  • Mesenchymal cells → bone/cartilage-forming cells

  • Produces heterotopic bone formation

  • Squamous/columnar metaplasia → epithelial metaplasia

Exam Pearl: Myositis ossificans is a classic example of connective tissue metaplasia with heterotopic bone formation.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৫) What is the another name of adaptive control?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Adaptive control is another term used for delayed negative feedback, in which the response develops gradually and acts to reduce the initial disturbance. Unlike rapid feedback mechanisms, adaptive control generally requires a longer time to produce its effect and is important in maintaining long-term physiological stability. Examples include regulation of blood pressure and body fluid composition through mechanisms that involve renal and hormonal responses. The key feature is that the system detects a deviation from the desired state and initiates changes that oppose that deviation. Rapid negative feedback, in contrast, acts quickly through mechanisms such as neural reflexes. Positive feedback amplifies rather than opposes the initial change and is therefore not considered adaptive control.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adaptive control → Delayed negative feedback

  • Negative feedback → Opposes the initial change

  • Rapid feedback → Often mediated by neural mechanisms

  • Delayed feedback → Often involves hormonal/renal mechanisms

  • Positive feedback → Amplifies the initial change

Exam Pearl: Adaptive control = delayed negative feedback.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৬) The antioxidant found in the body excludes—
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Serum albumin, transferrin, and ceruloplasmin are recognized components of the body's antioxidant defense system. Albumin contributes through its free thiol groups and by binding transition metals, particularly copper. Transferrin binds iron and prevents iron-mediated free-radical generation. Ceruloplasmin carries copper and has antioxidant activity through its ferroxidase function, helping prevent free iron from participating in oxidative reactions. Cobalamin (vitamin B12) is primarily involved in DNA synthesis and normal neurological function and is not classically listed among the major endogenous antioxidant proteins. Therefore, cobalamin is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Albumin → antioxidant + metal binding

  • Transferrin → binds iron

  • Ceruloplasmin → copper transport + ferroxidase activity

  • Cobalamin → vitamin B12, important for DNA synthesis and neurologic function

  • Major antioxidant enzymes → superoxide dismutase, catalase, glutathione peroxidase

Exam Pearl: Albumin, transferrin, and ceruloplasmin contribute to antioxidant defense; cobalamin is the exception here.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৭) Where perichondrium is absent?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Perichondrium is absent in fibrocartilage. Fibrocartilage contains abundant type I collagen bundles and is adapted to withstand high tensile and compressive forces. It is found in structures such as intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci. Hyaline cartilage generally has a perichondrium, except at specialized sites such as articular cartilage and the cartilage of the epiphyseal growth plate. Elastic cartilage is surrounded by a perichondrium. Because fibrocartilage lacks perichondrium, its nutrition depends primarily on diffusion from surrounding tissues. Therefore, among the given options, fibrocartilage is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Fibrocartilage → No perichondrium

  • Hyaline cartilage → Usually has perichondrium

  • Articular hyaline cartilage → No perichondrium

  • Elastic cartilage → Perichondrium present

  • Fibrocartilage → Type I collagen predominates

  • Fibrocartilage sites → IV disc, pubic symphysis, menisci

Exam Pearl: Fibrocartilage is classically the cartilage type without a perichondrium.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৮) Which one is the predominant inflammatory cell in viral infection?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Lymphocytes are the predominant inflammatory cells typically associated with viral infections. Viral infections stimulate both innate and adaptive immune responses, with T lymphocytes, particularly cytotoxic T cells, playing a major role in eliminating virus-infected cells. Histologically, viral infections commonly produce a predominantly mononuclear infiltrate consisting of lymphocytes, with variable numbers of macrophages and plasma cells. Neutrophils are more characteristic of acute bacterial infections, while eosinophils are associated mainly with allergic reactions and parasitic infections. Macrophages may also be prominent in viral infections, but lymphocytes are the classic exam answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Viral infection → Lymphocytes

  • Bacterial infection → Neutrophils

  • Parasitic infection/allergy → Eosinophils

  • Chronic inflammation → Lymphocytes + macrophages + plasma cells

  • Cytotoxic T cells are important in virus-infected cell killing

Exam Pearl: Viral infection classically produces a lymphocytic inflammatory infiltrate.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১৯) CO2 is transported from blood to alveoli by which of the following process?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
CO₂ moves from blood into the alveoli by simple diffusion down its partial-pressure gradient across the alveolar-capillary membrane. CO₂ produced by tissue metabolism is transported in blood mainly as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻), with smaller amounts dissolved in plasma and bound to proteins as carbamino compounds. In the pulmonary capillaries, bicarbonate is converted back to CO₂ within red blood cells, and the resulting CO₂ diffuses from pulmonary capillary blood into the alveolar air. This movement requires no ATP and no membrane transport protein, so it is classified as simple diffusion. Facilitated diffusion involves carrier proteins, while primary and secondary active transport require energy and are not involved in alveolar CO₂ elimination.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Blood → alveoli CO₂ → Simple diffusion

  • Driven by the CO₂ partial-pressure gradient

  • CO₂ is mainly transported as bicarbonate

  • No ATP is required

  • CO₂ diffuses across the alveolar-capillary membrane

Exam Pearl: Gas exchange of CO₂ between pulmonary blood and alveoli occurs by simple diffusion.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২০) Aschoff giant cell is found in---?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Aschoff giant cells are characteristic histological cells found in Aschoff bodies, the pathognomonic inflammatory lesions of rheumatic fever, particularly involving the heart in rheumatic carditis. They are large macrophage-derived cells with abundant cytoplasm and characteristic nuclear changes, including caterpillar-like chromatin. Aschoff bodies are found mainly in the myocardium and represent a delayed hypersensitivity reaction following infection with Group A Streptococcus. TB granulomas contain Langhans giant cells, while syphilis may show plasma-cell-rich inflammation and lymphoma is a neoplastic lymphoid disorder. Therefore, rheumatic heart disease is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aschoff body → Rheumatic fever/rheumatic carditis

  • Aschoff giant cell → Macrophage-derived

  • Characteristic nucleus → Caterpillar-like chromatin

  • TB → Langhans giant cells

  • Rheumatic fever follows Group A Streptococcal infection

Exam Pearl: Aschoff giant cell = rheumatic fever; Langhans giant cell = tuberculosis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২১) Which arises from diaphysis in long bone?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The diaphysis is the long, central portion of a long bone and is commonly referred to as the shaft. It consists mainly of compact bone surrounding the medullary cavity and provides structural strength and support. The epiphyses form the expanded ends of long bones, while the metaphysis lies between the diaphysis and epiphysis and contains the growth plate in growing individuals. Therefore, when asked which part of a long bone corresponds to the diaphysis, the correct answer is shaft. The head and neck are specific anatomical structures found at the ends of certain bones, such as the femur and humerus, rather than being synonymous with diaphysis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Diaphysis = Shaft

  • Epiphysis = End of long bone

  • Metaphysis = Region between diaphysis and epiphysis

  • Diaphysis → mainly compact bone

  • Medullary cavity → located mainly within the diaphysis

Exam Pearl: Diaphysis simply means the shaft of a long bon

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২২) Which is not permanent cell on the basis of regenerative capacity?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Based on regenerative capacity, cells are broadly classified as labile, stable, or permanent. Skeletal muscle cells are generally considered stable cells, because mature skeletal muscle fibers do not normally undergo cell division, but they have a limited capacity for regeneration through satellite cells. In contrast, neurons and cardiac muscle cells are classically regarded as permanent cells, with very limited regenerative capacity after significant injury. Smooth muscle cells are considered stable cells and can undergo proliferation, particularly in response to injury or hormonal stimuli. Therefore, among the options, skeletal muscle is the best answer if the question asks for a cell that is not permanent.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Permanent cells: Neurons, cardiac muscle cells

  • Stable cells: Skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, hepatocytes

  • Skeletal muscle regeneration → satellite cells

  • Labile cells: Epidermis, intestinal epithelium, bone marrow

  • Stable cells can proliferate when appropriately stimulated

Exam Pearl: Skeletal muscle is classically a stable cell population because satellite cells provide limited regenerative capacity.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৩) What cytoskeletal structure connects extracellular matrix to intracellular matrix?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Intermediate filaments provide a mechanical link between the extracellular matrix (ECM) and the intracellular cytoskeleton through cell adhesion structures, particularly hemidesmosomes. In epithelial cells, extracellular matrix components bind to integrins, which connect intracellularly to intermediate filaments, especially keratin. This arrangement allows mechanical forces to be transmitted from the ECM through the cell membrane to the cytoskeleton. Microfilaments (actin) also participate in cell–matrix adhesion through focal adhesions, but the classic structural connection emphasized in histology and cell biology is the intermediate filament–hemidesmosome system. Therefore, intermediate filament is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Intermediate filament → Hemidesmosome → ECM

  • Integrins are major cell–ECM adhesion receptors

  • Hemidesmosomes → connect cells to basement membrane

  • Focal adhesions → actin microfilaments + ECM

  • Intermediate filaments provide tensile strength

Exam Pearl: Think “hemidesmosome + intermediate filament” for the classic ECM-to-intracellular cytoskeletal connection.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৪) Generalized oedema is termed as –?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Anasarca refers to severe generalized edema involving the subcutaneous tissues and often multiple body compartments. It may occur in conditions such as congestive heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, severe renal disease, and advanced liver disease, usually due to increased hydrostatic pressure, reduced plasma oncotic pressure, sodium and water retention, or increased vascular permeability. Ascites specifically refers to fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity. Hydrothorax refers to fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity, while pleural effusion is the general term for abnormal fluid accumulation in the pleural space. Therefore, generalized edema is termed anasarca.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Generalized severe edema → Anasarca

  • Peritoneal fluid → Ascites

  • Pleural fluid → Pleural effusion / hydrothorax

  • Nephrotic syndrome → edema due to hypoalbuminemia

  • Heart failure → edema mainly due to increased hydrostatic pressure

Exam Pearl: Anasarca = generalized, severe edema of the body.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৫) What type of joint is present in between teeth and socket?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Gomphosis is a specialized fibrous joint that connects a tooth to its bony socket (alveolus). The tooth is attached to the socket by the periodontal ligament, which consists of dense connective tissue fibers extending between the cementum of the tooth and the alveolar bone. Gomphosis is considered a peg-and-socket type of fibrous joint and provides both firm attachment and slight movement of the tooth under mechanical forces. Symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint, syndesmosis is a fibrous joint connecting bones by ligaments or membranes, and suture is a fibrous joint found between the bones of the skull.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Tooth + socket → Gomphosis

  • Gomphosis → Fibrous joint

  • Connecting structure → Periodontal ligament

  • Syndesmosis → Bones connected by ligament/interosseous membrane

  • Suture → Fibrous joint between skull bones

Exam Pearl: Gomphosis = tooth anchored in its socket.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৬) Karyotype of turner’s syndrome is--?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by complete or partial absence of one X chromosome, classically represented by the karyotype 45,X (often written as 45,XO in exam questions). Affected individuals are phenotypically female and commonly have short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, primary amenorrhea, and infertility. The other options represent different chromosomal abnormalities: 47,XXY is Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XX,+21 is Down syndrome, and 47,XX,+18 is Edwards syndrome. Therefore, 45,XO is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Turner syndrome → 45,X

  • Phenotypic sex → Female

  • Classic features → Short stature + ovarian failure + infertility

  • Klinefelter → 47,XXY

  • Down syndrome → Trisomy 21

  • Edwards syndrome → Trisomy 18

Exam Pearl: Turner = 45,X; Klinefelter = 47,XXY.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৭) Which of the following is the best index of platelet function?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Bleeding time is a traditional clinical test that assesses primary hemostasis, particularly platelet number and function, along with the interaction between platelets and the vessel wall. Therefore, among the given options, it is the best index of platelet function. Clotting time mainly assesses the intrinsic coagulation pathway, while prothrombin time (PT) assesses the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. Clot retraction depends on platelet function, particularly platelet contractile activity, but it is not the standard overall screening test for platelet function in this context. Thus, bleeding time is the accepted exam answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Platelet function → Bleeding time

  • PT → Extrinsic + common pathway

  • aPTT → Intrinsic + common pathway

  • Platelets → Primary hemostasis

  • Clot retraction → Depends significantly on platelet function

Exam Pearl: Bleeding time is the classic exam test for platelet function.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৮) Which is not oncogenic virus??
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
HIV is not itself considered a directly oncogenic virus. Instead, HIV causes profound immunosuppression, particularly through depletion of CD4⁺ T lymphocytes, which increases susceptibility to cancers caused by other oncogenic viruses. In contrast, HPV is directly oncogenic and is strongly associated with cervical and several anogenital and oropharyngeal cancers. EBV is associated with Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and some Hodgkin and other lymphomas. HBV is an oncogenic virus associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, partly through chronic inflammation and other mechanisms. HIV therefore represents the best answer among the given options.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • HPV → Cervical carcinoma

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma

  • HBV → Hepatocellular carcinoma

  • HIV → Immunodeficiency; not directly oncogenic

  • HIV increases cancer risk mainly through immunosuppression

Exam Pearl: HIV promotes malignancy indirectly through immunosuppression; it is not classified as a directly oncogenic virus.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ২৯) Where spermatogenesis occurs?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Spermatogenesis is the process by which spermatogonia develop into mature spermatozoa, and it occurs within the seminiferous tubules of the testes. The seminiferous epithelium contains developing germ cells supported by Sertoli cells. Spermatogenesis includes mitotic proliferation of spermatogonia, meiosis of spermatocytes, and spermiogenesis, during which spermatids differentiate into spermatozoa. The epididymis is primarily responsible for sperm maturation, storage, and acquisition of motility, not sperm production. The rete testis and ejaculatory duct mainly function in the transport of sperm. Therefore, the seminiferous tubules are the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spermatogenesis → Seminiferous tubules

  • Sertoli cells → Support developing germ cells

  • Leydig cells → Produce testosterone

  • Epididymis → Sperm maturation and storage

  • Rete testis → Sperm transport

Exam Pearl: Spermatogenesis occurs in the seminiferous tubules of the testes.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩০) What is the nature of lymph node in Hodgkin's lymphoma?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
In Hodgkin lymphoma, the affected lymph nodes are classically described as firm, rubbery, and non-tender. They are usually painless and may form matted or contiguous groups, particularly in the cervical and mediastinal regions. The characteristic “rubbery” consistency is due to the cellular infiltrate and altered lymph node architecture caused by the lymphoma. A hard lymph node is more suggestive of metastatic carcinoma, while soft nodes may occur in some inflammatory or infective conditions. Therefore, among the given options, rubbery is the classic exam description of lymph nodes in Hodgkin lymphoma.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hodgkin lymphoma → Rubbery, non-tender lymph nodes

  • Usually painless

  • Commonly involves cervical lymph nodes

  • Mediastinal lymphadenopathy is common

  • Hard, irregular nodes → think metastatic carcinoma

Exam Pearl: “Rubbery, painless lymph node” is a classic clinical clue for Hodgkin lymphoma.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩১) Bacterial spores are destroyed by following process excludes...?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Boiling does not reliably destroy bacterial spores, making it the correct answer for “excludes.” Bacterial endospores are highly resistant to heat and can survive ordinary boiling at 100°C, although prolonged boiling may reduce the number of viable spores. Autoclaving uses moist heat under pressure, typically 121°C, and is an effective method for destroying bacterial spores. A hot-air oven uses dry heat at sufficiently high temperatures and exposure times to achieve sterilization, including destruction of spores. Gamma radiation is also an effective sterilization method and can destroy bacterial spores through DNA damage. Therefore, boiling is not a reliable sporicidal sterilization method.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Boiling → Not reliable for spores

  • Autoclave → Moist heat under pressure

  • Hot-air oven → Dry heat sterilization

  • Gamma radiation → Effective sterilization method

  • Bacterial spores → Highly resistant to heat and chemicals

Exam Pearl: Boiling kills many vegetative bacteria but does not reliably destroy bacterial spores.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩২) Triple response does not include---?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The triple response of Lewis is a local vascular response to mechanical injury or stroking of the skin. It consists of three sequential components: red reaction, flare, and wheal. The red reaction occurs due to local capillary dilatation, the flare is caused by arteriolar dilatation mediated by an axon reflex, and the wheal results from increased capillary permeability with local edema. The white reaction is not part of the classic triple response. Therefore, among the given options, white reaction is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Triple response of Lewis → Red reaction + Flare + Wheal

  • Red reaction → Capillary dilatation

  • Flare → Axon reflex

  • Wheal → Increased vascular permeability

  • White reaction → Not part of triple response

Exam Pearl: Lewis triple response = Red + Flare + Wheal.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৩) Filtration is suitable method for sterilization of.....?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Filtration is an appropriate sterilization method for heat-sensitive liquids, particularly IV fluids, biological solutions, and some pharmaceutical preparations that may be damaged by heat. Membrane filters physically remove microorganisms, including bacteria, from the liquid without exposing the solution to high temperatures. Surgical gauzes are typically sterilized by methods such as autoclaving. Catheters may be sterilized using methods appropriate to their material, including ethylene oxide or other validated methods. Culture media are commonly sterilized by autoclaving, although heat-sensitive components may require filtration and aseptic addition. Therefore, among the given options, IV fluid is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Filtration → Heat-sensitive liquids

  • IV fluids → Common example

  • Filtration removes microorganisms physically

  • Autoclave → Commonly used for culture media

  • Surgical gauze → Commonly sterilized by moist heat

Exam Pearl: Filter sterilization is preferred for heat-sensitive fluids such as IV solutions.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৪) Which plasma protein responsible for transport of Cu?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Ceruloplasmin, an α₂-globulin, is the major plasma protein responsible for transporting copper (Cu) in the blood. It carries approximately 90–95% of circulating copper. A small amount of copper is also loosely bound to albumin, but ceruloplasmin is the principal copper-transport protein. Fibrinogen is primarily involved in blood coagulation, while prothrombin is a vitamin K–dependent clotting factor that is converted to thrombin during coagulation. Therefore, among the given options, globulin is the best answer because ceruloplasmin belongs to the globulin fraction.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Copper transport → Ceruloplasmin

  • Ceruloplasmin → α₂-globulin

  • Most plasma copper → Bound to ceruloplasmin

  • Albumin → Binds a smaller fraction of copper

  • Fibrinogen → Clotting protein

  • Prothrombin → Factor II

Exam Pearl: Ceruloplasmin is an α₂-globulin and the principal plasma transporter of copper.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৫) All of the following endocrine disorders causes shock except...... ?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Cushing's syndrome is not a typical cause of shock because excess cortisol generally produces hypertension, increased vascular responsiveness to catecholamines, and fluid retention. In contrast, severe hypothyroidism can cause myxedema coma with hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, and shock. Hyperthyroidism, particularly thyroid storm, may cause cardiovascular collapse and shock due to severe tachycardia, arrhythmias, and high-output cardiac failure. Addison's disease can cause an acute adrenal crisis characterized by profound hypotension and hypovolemic/distributive shock due to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency. Therefore, Cushing's syndrome is the exception.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Addisonian crisis → Shock + hypotension

  • Myxedema coma → Hypotension/shock

  • Thyroid storm → Cardiovascular collapse/shock

  • Cushing's syndrome → Usually hypertension

  • Cortisol deficiency → Reduced vascular responsiveness to catecholamines

Exam Pearl: Cushing's syndrome causes hypertension; adrenal insufficiency causes shock.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৬) By which process conditioning of sperm in female genital tract occurs?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Capacitation is the functional maturation or “conditioning” of sperm that occurs after ejaculation within the female genital tract. During capacitation, biochemical and membrane changes occur in the sperm, including removal of surface glycoproteins and seminal plasma proteins, changes in membrane fluidity, and development of hyperactivated motility. These changes enable the sperm to undergo the acrosome reaction and successfully penetrate the zona pellucida during fertilization. Spermiogenesis is the maturation of spermatids into spermatozoa within the testes. Implantation is the attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium, while fertilization is the fusion of sperm and ovum.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sperm conditioning in female genital tract → Capacitation

  • Capacitation occurs mainly in the female reproductive tract

  • Enables acrosome reaction

  • Spermiogenesis → Spermatid → Spermatozoon

  • Fertilization → Fusion of sperm and oocyte

Exam Pearl: Capacitation = functional conditioning of sperm in the female genital tract.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৭) Treatment of enteric fever should be continued for how many days?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
For uncomplicated enteric (typhoid) fever, antibiotic treatment is commonly continued for about 10 days, depending on the antibiotic used, clinical response, and local antimicrobial resistance patterns. Historically, longer courses such as 14 days were used, but shorter effective regimens are now widely accepted with appropriate antibiotics. For example, ceftriaxone is often given for approximately 10–14 days, while azithromycin may be used for shorter courses. Therefore, in a standard single-best-answer examination question without specifying the antibiotic, 10 days is the best answer among the options. Treatment duration should ultimately be individualized according to the drug, severity, complications, and clinical response.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enteric fever treatment → commonly about 10 days

  • Duration varies with antibiotic and clinical response

  • Ceftriaxone → often 10–14 days

  • Azithromycin → usually shorter course

  • Complicated disease → may require longer treatment

Exam Pearl: For a general exam question, remember enteric fever treatment is classically around 10 days.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৮) The area between two adjacent Z lines is called---?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
A sarcomere is the basic structural and functional unit of a striated muscle fiber. It extends from one Z line (Z disc) to the next adjacent Z line. Each sarcomere contains thin actin filaments anchored to the Z discs and thick myosin filaments located centrally. During muscle contraction, the actin filaments slide toward the M line, causing shortening of the sarcomere without shortening of the individual thick or thin filaments. A myofibril is composed of many sarcomeres arranged end-to-end, whereas myofilaments refer to actin and myosin filaments themselves. Therefore, the area between two adjacent Z lines is a sarcomere.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Z line to Z line → Sarcomere

  • Sarcomere → Functional unit of striated muscle

  • Thin filament → Actin

  • Thick filament → Myosin

  • Myofibril → Long chain of sarcomeres

Exam Pearl: One sarcomere = the segment between two adjacent Z discs.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৩৯) Spider web clot of CSF found in which type of meningitis?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
A spider-web (cobweb) clot forming in the CSF after standing is a classic finding of tuberculous meningitis. The CSF typically shows a raised protein concentration, low glucose, and predominantly lymphocytic pleocytosis. When the CSF is allowed to stand, the high protein content can form a delicate fibrin web or cobweb-like clot, in which tubercle bacilli may sometimes be detected. In acute bacterial meningitis, CSF typically shows neutrophilic pleocytosis, markedly raised protein, and low glucose, but a spider-web clot is not the classic finding. Viral meningitis generally has normal glucose and lymphocytic predominance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Spider-web/cobweb clot → Tuberculous meningitis

  • TB meningitis → Lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose

  • Bacterial meningitis → Neutrophils + high protein + low glucose

  • Viral meningitis → Lymphocytes + usually normal glucose

  • Cobweb clot results from fibrin formation

Exam Pearl: Spider-web clot in CSF = Tuberculous meningitis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪০) The process cleavage occurs in which week of development?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Cleavage is the series of rapid mitotic divisions of the zygote that occurs during the first week of embryonic development. It begins shortly after fertilization as the zygote travels through the uterine tube toward the uterus. The successive divisions produce smaller cells called blastomeres, progressing through the 2-cell, 4-cell, 8-cell stages and eventually forming the morula. The morula then develops into a blastocyst, which reaches the uterine cavity around day 5. Implantation begins during the second week. Therefore, cleavage is classically considered a process of the first week of development.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cleavage → 1st week

  • Zygote → Blastomeres → Morula → Blastocyst

  • Cleavage consists of rapid mitotic divisions

  • Morula → approximately day 3

  • Blastocyst → approximately day 5

  • Implantation → begins in the 2nd week

Exam Pearl: Week 1 = cleavage, morula and blastocyst formation; Week 2 = implantation.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪১) Which ranks 1st among the cause of death in ICU?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Septic shock is a major and commonly cited cause of death among critically ill patients in the ICU. It represents severe infection-associated circulatory and cellular dysfunction, leading to persistent hypotension, impaired tissue perfusion, and multiorgan dysfunction despite adequate fluid resuscitation. Systemic inflammatory responses cause widespread vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, myocardial dysfunction, and abnormalities of cellular oxygen utilization. MI and stroke are major causes of mortality overall, but in the ICU context, sepsis and septic shock are among the leading causes of death. Anaphylactic shock is potentially fatal but is much less common as a cause of ICU mortality.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Septic shock → Major cause of ICU mortality

  • Septic shock → Infection + circulatory/metabolic dysfunction

  • Major mechanism → Vasodilation + capillary leak + tissue hypoperfusion

  • Severe sepsis can cause multiorgan dysfunction

  • Anaphylactic shock → IgE-mediated distributive shock

Exam Pearl: Among the given options, septic shock is the best answer for the leading ICU cause of death.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪২) RBC does not contain which of the following?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Mature red blood cells (RBCs) contain several intracellular enzymes, including G6PD, AST, and LDH, which are important in maintaining cellular metabolism and antioxidant defense. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP), however, is not a significant enzyme component of mature RBCs. G6PD is particularly important because it generates NADPH, helping RBCs maintain reduced glutathione and protect against oxidative damage. LDH is abundant in RBCs because they depend entirely on anaerobic glycolysis for ATP production. AST is also present intracellularly. Therefore, among the given options, ALP is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RBC contains G6PD

  • RBC contains LDH

  • RBC contains AST

  • ALP is not present as a significant RBC enzyme

  • Hemolysis can increase measured LDH and AST

Exam Pearl: RBC contains G6PD, AST and LDH; ALP is the exception.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৩) Which of the following is not a cause of reactionary haemorrhage?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Reactionary haemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours after surgery, commonly due to slippage of a ligature, dislodgement of a clot, or normalization of blood pressure after the initial postoperative hypotension. These factors can cause bleeding from a previously controlled vessel. Infection is a recognized cause of secondary haemorrhage, which typically occurs several days after surgery due to erosion of a blood vessel by infection. Therefore, infection is not a typical cause of reactionary haemorrhage and is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Reactionary haemorrhage → Usually within 24 hours

  • Causes → Ligature slip, clot dislodgement, rise/normalization of BP

  • Secondary haemorrhage → Usually 7–14 days, often due to infection

  • Primary haemorrhage → Occurs immediately during/after surgery

Exam Pearl: Infection causes secondary haemorrhage, not reactionary haemorrhage.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৪) Paterson Brown kelly syndrome excludes.....?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Plummer–Vinson syndrome (Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome) is classically characterized by iron deficiency anemia (IDA), dysphagia, and esophageal webs. Iron deficiency may also cause mucosal changes, including angular stomatitis and atrophic changes of the oral mucosa. Glossitis can occur in iron deficiency and may be described in some clinical sources, but it is not part of the classic diagnostic triad. Therefore, for a single-best-answer examination question asking what is excluded from the classic features of Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome, glossitis is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Plummer–Vinson syndrome → IDA + dysphagia + esophageal webs

  • Also called Paterson–Brown–Kelly syndrome

  • Angular stomatitis → Associated with iron deficiency

  • Esophageal webs → Typically in the upper esophagus

  • Associated with increased risk of upper aerodigestive tract squamous cell carcinoma

Exam Pearl: Remember the triad: Iron deficiency anemia + dysphagia + esophageal web.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৫) What is the source of development of neuroglia?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Most neuroglial cells develop from the neuroectoderm of the neural tube. Astrocytes and oligodendrocytes arise from neuroepithelial cells of the neural tube, while ependymal cells also develop from its neuroepithelium. However, there is an important exception: microglia are derived from mesodermal/yolk-sac macrophage precursors. Some peripheral glial cells, such as Schwann cells and satellite cells, arise from the neural crest. Therefore, although the question is somewhat broad, the accepted examination answer for the principal source of neuroglia is the neural tube.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Astrocytes → Neural tube

  • Oligodendrocytes → Neural tube

  • Ependymal cells → Neural tube

  • Microglia → Mesoderm/yolk sac

  • Schwann cells → Neural crest

  • Satellite cells → Neural crest

Exam Pearl: Most CNS neuroglia arise from the neural tube; microglia are the key mesodermal exception.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৬) Which one is the most common cause of genital ulcer?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Genital herpes, caused predominantly by herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV-2), is the most common cause of genital ulceration among sexually transmitted infections. It typically produces multiple painful vesicles that rupture to form shallow, painful ulcers, often accompanied by local tenderness and sometimes systemic symptoms during the first episode. Primary syphilis classically causes a single, painless, indurated chancre, whereas chancroid causes painful ulcers with ragged edges and is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi. Granuloma inguinale produces painless, progressive beefy-red ulcers that bleed easily. Therefore, genital herpes is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common genital ulcer disease → Genital herpes

  • Herpes → Painful, multiple ulcers

  • Primary syphilis → Painless, indurated chancre

  • Chancroid → Painful, ragged ulcer

  • Granuloma inguinale → Beefy-red, friable ulcer

Exam Pearl: Painful multiple genital ulcers strongly suggest genital herpes.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৭) The ECG waves are predominantly negative in which of the following?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The ECG complex is predominantly negative in lead aVR because the normal electrical depolarization of the heart generally travels away from the positive electrode of aVR. The positive electrode of aVR is directed toward the right shoulder, whereas the mean cardiac electrical axis normally points approximately toward the left and inferiorly. Therefore, the main P wave, QRS complex, and T wave are usually negative in aVR. In contrast, lead II and aVF generally show predominantly positive QRS complexes because they view electrical activity moving toward their positive electrodes. aVL may be positive or variable depending on the individual’s cardiac axis.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • aVR → Usually predominantly negative

  • Lead II → Usually positive P, QRS, and T

  • aVF → Usually positive QRS

  • aVR looks toward the right shoulder

  • Normal mean QRS axis → Approximately −30° to +90°

Exam Pearl: Remember: aVR is normally the “negative-looking” limb lead.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৮) Pappenheimer bodies are found in---?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Pappenheimer bodies are abnormal iron-containing granules within red blood cells. They represent aggregates of ferritin or hemosiderin and are demonstrated with a Prussian blue stain. They are classically associated with sideroblastic anemia, where defective heme synthesis causes iron accumulation in erythroid precursors. Pappenheimer bodies may also be seen in other conditions involving impaired splenic function or abnormal erythropoiesis, but sideroblastic anemia is the classic examination association. In contrast, Howell–Jolly bodies are nuclear DNA remnants commonly seen after splenectomy, while basophilic stippling represents aggregated ribosomal RNA and is classically associated with lead poisoning.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pappenheimer bodies → Sideroblastic anemia

  • Contain iron

  • Demonstrated by Prussian blue stain

  • Howell–Jolly bodies → DNA remnants

  • Basophilic stippling → Aggregated ribosomal RNA

  • Sideroblastic anemia → Ring sideroblasts in bone marrow

Exam Pearl: Pappenheimer bodies = iron granules inside RBCs = sideroblastic anemia.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৪৯) What is the source of development of prostate?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The **prostate gland develops from endodermal epithelial buds arising from the prostatic part of the urogenital sinus. These buds grow into the surrounding mesenchyme and differentiate to form the glandular epithelium of the prostate, while the surrounding mesenchyme contributes to its smooth muscle and connective tissue stroma. The ureteric bud develops mainly into the ureter, renal pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts. The mesonephric duct contributes to structures such as the epididymal duct, ductus deferens, and ejaculatory duct in males. The paramesonephric duct contributes mainly to female reproductive tract structures. Therefore, the urogenital sinus is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Prostate → Urogenital sinus

  • Prostate epithelium → Endoderm

  • Ureteric bud → Collecting system of kidney

  • Mesonephric duct → Epididymis and ductus deferens

  • Paramesonephric duct → Uterine tubes, uterus, upper vagina

Exam Pearl: Prostate gland develops from endodermal buds of the urogenital sinus.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫০) Estimation of red cell lifespan is done by use of radioactive --?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The lifespan of red blood cells can be estimated by labeling them with radioactive chromium-51 (⁵¹Cr). In the ⁵¹Cr red-cell survival study, the patient’s RBCs are labeled ex vivo and then reinfused. The decline in circulating radioactivity over time is used to estimate RBC survival and lifespan. Normally, RBC lifespan is approximately 120 days. Cobalt-60 is mainly associated with radiotherapy and does not serve as the standard tracer for RBC survival. Radioactive carbon may be used in other metabolic studies, while radioactive iodine is primarily used for thyroid function and imaging.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • RBC lifespan → Chromium-51 (⁵¹Cr)

  • Normal RBC lifespan → ~120 days

  • ⁵¹Cr → Used for RBC survival studies

  • Radioactive iodine → Thyroid studies

  • Cobalt-60 → Radiotherapy

Exam Pearl: ⁵¹Cr labeling is the classic method for estimating red-cell lifespan.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫১) What will be the finding of hand examination in hyperthyroidism?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
In hyperthyroidism, increased thyroid hormone raises the basal metabolic rate and increases heat production. To dissipate this excess heat, cutaneous blood flow and sweating increase, producing warm or hot, moist/sweaty hands. Patients may also have a fine tremor, warm skin, and palmar erythema. In contrast, hypothyroidism typically causes cold, dry, coarse skin due to reduced metabolic activity and reduced sweating. Therefore, among the given options, hot, sweaty hands are the characteristic finding in hyperthyroidism.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyperthyroidism → Hot, sweaty hands

  • Fine tremor → Common finding

  • Increased heat production → Warm skin

  • Hypothyroidism → Cold, dry, coarse skin

  • Hyperthyroidism → Increased sweating and peripheral blood flow

Exam Pearl: Hyperthyroidism = warm, moist skin with sweaty hands.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫২) Which is intermediate acting BP control mechanism?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The baroreceptor mechanism is the principal intermediate-term mechanism for regulation of arterial blood pressure. It acts within seconds to minutes through stretch receptors located mainly in the carotid sinus and aortic arch. Changes in arterial pressure alter baroreceptor firing, which modifies sympathetic and parasympathetic activity, producing changes in heart rate, cardiac contractility, and peripheral vascular resistance. In contrast, the CNS ischemic response is an extremely rapid emergency mechanism that becomes important during severe hypotension. The capillary fluid shift mechanism acts over minutes to hours, while renal-body fluid mechanisms are important for long-term regulation. Therefore, baroreceptor reflex is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rapid BP control → Baroreceptor reflex

  • Baroreceptors → Carotid sinus + aortic arch

  • Intermediate-term → Baroreceptor mechanism

  • Long-term BP control → Renal-body fluid mechanism

  • CNS ischemic response → Powerful emergency mechanism

Exam Pearl: Baroreceptor reflex is the classic intermediate-term regulator of arterial blood pressure.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৩) JAK2 mutation is a characteristic feature of...?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The JAK2 V617F mutation is a characteristic molecular abnormality of polycythemia vera (PRV) and is present in the great majority of patients. JAK2 is a tyrosine kinase involved in signaling through several hematopoietic growth-factor receptors. The mutation causes constitutive activation of the JAK-STAT pathway, leading to growth-factor-independent myeloid proliferation, particularly increased red-cell production. JAK2 mutations are also found in many cases of essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis, so the question is somewhat ambiguous if interpreted broadly. However, among the given options, PRV is the classic single-best exam answer. CML is instead characteristically associated with the BCR-ABL1 fusion gene.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Polycythemia vera → JAK2 V617F

  • Essential thrombocythemia → JAK2/CALR/MPL mutations

  • Primary myelofibrosis → JAK2/CALR/MPL mutations

  • CML → BCR-ABL1

  • JAK2 mutation → Constitutive JAK-STAT activation

Exam Pearl: PRV is classically associated with JAK2 V617

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৪) Common carotid artery develops from ...... arch?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The common carotid arteries develop mainly from the third aortic arches. The third aortic arch gives rise to the common carotid arteries and the proximal portions of the internal carotid arteries. The distal part of the internal carotid artery develops from the cranial portion of the dorsal aorta. The external carotid arteries develop as sprouts from the third aortic arch region. The first and second aortic arches largely regress, contributing only to small vascular remnants, while the fourth arch contributes to different structures, including part of the aortic arch on the left and proximal right subclavian artery on the right.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • 3rd aortic arch → Common carotid + proximal internal carotid

  • Internal carotid distal part → Dorsal aorta

  • External carotid → Sprout from 3rd arch region

  • 4th arch (left) → Part of aortic arch

  • 4th arch (right) → Part of right subclavian artery

Exam Pearl: Third aortic arch = carotid arteries.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৫) Which anticoagulant is not used in blood transfusion?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
EDTA is not used as an anticoagulant for routine blood collection and storage for transfusion because it strongly chelates calcium and can adversely affect cellular function and red-cell viability during storage. Blood banks use citrate-based anticoagulant-preservative solutions such as ACD (acid-citrate-dextrose) and CPD (citrate-phosphate-dextrose). Disodium citrate also acts as an anticoagulant by binding ionized calcium and has been used in blood preservation and transfusion-related settings. Therefore, among the options, EDTA is the anticoagulant not used for blood transfusion.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Blood transfusion anticoagulants → Citrate-based

  • ACD → Acid-citrate-dextrose

  • CPD → Citrate-phosphate-dextrose

  • Citrate → Anticoagulates by chelating calcium

  • EDTA → Mainly used for hematology blood samples

Exam Pearl: EDTA is for laboratory hematology samples; citrate-based solutions are used for stored blood.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৬) Which is known as capacitance vessels?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Veins are known as capacitance vessels because they are highly compliant and can accommodate a large volume of blood with relatively small changes in venous pressure. The systemic venous system contains approximately 60–70% of the total blood volume at rest and therefore serves as the major blood reservoir. Venous smooth muscle tone is regulated by sympathetic activity, which can mobilize stored blood toward the heart during exercise or hemorrhage. Arteries are primarily pressure vessels, arterioles are resistance vessels, and capillaries are the principal exchange vessels.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Veins → Capacitance vessels

  • Arteries → Pressure vessels

  • Arterioles → Resistance vessels

  • Capillaries → Exchange vessels

  • Veins contain the largest proportion of circulating blood volume

Exam Pearl: Veins = capacitance (blood reservoir) vessels.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৭) Which one is the most important cause of NGU?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the most important and common cause of nongonococcal urethritis (NGU). It is responsible for a substantial proportion of NGU cases, particularly in younger sexually active individuals. Chlamydial urethritis typically presents with dysuria and a scanty or mucoid urethral discharge. Mycoplasma genitalium is another important cause of NGU, but it is not included among the options. Ureaplasma urealyticum may be associated with NGU, but its causal role is less consistent. Trichomonas vaginalis can cause urethritis but is not the principal cause, while herpes simplex virus is an uncommon cause.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most important cause of NGU → Chlamydia trachomatis

  • Gonococcal urethritis → Neisseria gonorrhoeae

  • Important non-chlamydial cause → Mycoplasma genitalium

  • Chlamydial urethritis → Dysuria + scanty/mucoid discharge

  • Ureaplasma → Possible association, but less consistent

Exam Pearl: NGU: think Chlamydia first; Mycoplasma genitalium is the major alternative.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৮) Which are typical intercostal nerve?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The typical intercostal nerves are T3–T6, which correspond to the 3rd to 6th intercostal nerves. They run in the costal groove between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles and supply the intercostal muscles, overlying skin, and parietal pleura. The 1st intercostal nerve is atypical because it largely contributes to the brachial plexus. The 2nd intercostal nerve is also atypical because its lateral cutaneous branch forms the intercostobrachial nerve. T7–T11 continue beyond the costal margin as thoracoabdominal nerves, while T12 is the subcostal nerve. Therefore, T3–T6 is the standard answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Typical intercostal nerves → T3–T6

  • T1 → Contributes to brachial plexus

  • T2 → Gives intercostobrachial nerve

  • T7–T11 → Thoracoabdominal nerves

  • T12 → Subcostal nerve

Exam Pearl: Typical intercostal nerves = T3, T4, T5, T6.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৫৯) Which is not a cardinal presentation of AGN?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) typically presents as a nephritic syndrome characterized by hematuria, oliguria, hypertension, and edema. Hematuria is often the most prominent urinary finding and may produce smoky or cola-colored urine. Oliguria results from reduced glomerular filtration, while sodium and water retention contribute to hypertension and edema. Hyperlipidemia is not a cardinal feature of AGN; it is more characteristic of nephrotic syndrome, where heavy proteinuria leads to hypoalbuminemia and compensatory increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis. Therefore, hyperlipidemia is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • AGN → Hematuria + oliguria + hypertension + edema

  • Nephritic syndrome → Hematuria predominates

  • Nephrotic syndrome → Heavy proteinuria + hypoalbuminemia + hyperlipidemia + edema

  • AGN → Reduced GFR

  • Hyperlipidemia → Strongly associated with nephrotic syndrome

Exam Pearl: Nephritic = hematuria; nephrotic = proteinuria + hyperlipidemia.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬০) Which of the following has highest pressure?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Among the given options, the pulmonary artery has the highest pressure. Although pulmonary arterial pressure is much lower than systemic arterial pressure, it is still considerably higher than the pressures in the left atrium, right atrium, and superior vena cava. Normal pulmonary artery pressure is approximately 25/8 mmHg, with a mean pressure around 15 mmHg. Left atrial pressure is usually around 5–12 mmHg, while right atrial and SVC pressures are generally only a few mmHg. Therefore, pulmonary artery has the highest pressure among the listed vessels/chambers.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Pulmonary artery → ~25/8 mmHg

  • Left atrium → ~5–12 mmHg

  • Right atrium → ~0–5 mmHg

  • SVC → Low venous pressure

  • Systemic arterial pressure → Much higher, approximately 120/80 mmHg

Exam Pearl: Among these options, pulmonary artery has the highest pressure.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬১) Which is the cause of sterile pyuria?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Sterile pyuria means the presence of white blood cells in urine without growth of conventional bacteria on routine urine culture. Renal tuberculosis is a classic and important cause because Mycobacterium tuberculosis is not detected by routine bacterial culture methods. Other causes include sexually transmitted infections, interstitial nephritis, urinary stones, and partially treated bacterial UTI. CKD, AKI, and acute glomerulonephritis may produce urinary abnormalities, but they are not classic causes of sterile pyuria. Therefore, renal TB is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Sterile pyuria → Renal TB

  • Routine urine culture → Usually negative in TB

  • Other causes → Chlamydia, interstitial nephritis, renal stones

  • Renal TB may cause hematuria and urinary frequency

  • Persistent sterile pyuria → Consider genitourinary TB

Exam Pearl: Sterile pyuria + negative routine culture = think renal/genitourinary TB.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬২) Which is a cause of bilateral facial nerve palsy?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an important cause of bilateral facial nerve palsy, particularly in its classic acute inflammatory demyelinating form. Cranial nerve involvement occurs in GBS, with the facial nerve (CN VII) commonly affected, and facial weakness may be bilateral. Bell's palsy usually causes unilateral lower motor neuron facial paralysis, although bilateral cases can rarely occur. Parotid tumors typically cause unilateral facial nerve palsy due to local nerve involvement. Herpes zoster oticus (Ramsay Hunt syndrome) usually produces unilateral facial palsy associated with vesicular lesions around the ear. Therefore, GBS is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Bilateral facial palsy → Think GBS

  • GBS → Acute immune-mediated polyradiculoneuropathy

  • Facial nerve is a commonly affected cranial nerve

  • Bell's palsy → Usually unilateral

  • Parotid tumor → Usually unilateral facial weakness

  • Ramsay Hunt syndrome → Ipsilateral facial palsy + ear vesicles

Exam Pearl: Bilateral facial palsy is a classic cranial nerve association of GBS.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৩) Aspiration of pleural fluid is usually done through...... intercostal space?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Pleural fluid aspiration (thoracentesis) is classically performed through the 8th intercostal space, usually in the midaxillary or posterior axillary region, depending on the site and amount of fluid. The needle is introduced just above the upper border of the rib to avoid the main intercostal neurovascular bundle that runs along the inferior border of the rib. The needle should not be inserted too low because of the risk of injury to the diaphragm and abdominal organs. In modern practice, ultrasound guidance is preferred to identify a safe fluid pocket and reduce complications. For this standard anatomy MCQ, the best answer is the 8th intercostal space.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Thoracentesis → 8th intercostal space (classic exam answer)

  • Needle → Just above the upper border of the rib

  • Main intercostal neurovascular bundle → Along inferior border of rib

  • Ultrasound guidance → Preferred in modern practice

  • Avoid very low puncture → Risk of diaphragm/abdominal organ injury

Exam Pearl: Thoracentesis: 8th intercostal space, just above the rib.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৪) Pain during ejaculation signifies.....?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Painful ejaculation (odynorgasmia) is classically associated with prostatitis, particularly chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome. Inflammation of the prostate can cause pain during or immediately after ejaculation because the prostate and surrounding structures contract during ejaculation. Patients may also have perineal or pelvic pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, and painful ejaculation. Urethritis typically causes dysuria and urethral discharge, while cystitis mainly produces urinary frequency, urgency, and dysuria. Proctitis primarily causes rectal pain, tenesmus, and rectal discharge. Therefore, prostatitis is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Painful ejaculation → Prostatitis

  • Prostatitis → Perineal/pelvic pain + urinary symptoms

  • Urethritis → Dysuria + urethral discharge

  • Cystitis → Frequency + urgency + dysuria

  • Proctitis → Rectal pain + tenesmus

Exam Pearl: Pain during ejaculation = think prostatitis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৫) What is the main muscle of quiet inspiration?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The diaphragm is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration. When it contracts, its dome flattens and moves downward, increasing the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. This increases thoracic volume and lowers intrathoracic pressure, allowing air to flow into the lungs. The external intercostal muscles assist by elevating the ribs and increasing thoracic dimensions, but the diaphragm provides the major contribution during normal quiet breathing. The sternocleidomastoid is an accessory muscle recruited during deep or labored inspiration. The internal intercostals are primarily involved in forced expiration, although their interchondral portion can assist inspiration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Quiet inspiration → Diaphragm

  • Diaphragm contraction → Increases thoracic volume

  • External intercostals → Assist inspiration

  • Sternocleidomastoid → Accessory muscle of forced inspiration

  • Internal intercostals → Mainly forced expiration

Exam Pearl: Diaphragm is the principal muscle of quiet inspiration.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৬) Which is the most common cause of PUO?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Infection is the most common overall cause of pyrexia of unknown origin (PUO/FUO). Important infectious causes include tuberculosis, occult abscesses, endocarditis, and other deep-seated infections. The major diagnostic categories of FUO are infections, malignancies, non-infectious inflammatory/connective-tissue diseases, and miscellaneous causes. The relative frequency varies with age, geography, and patient population; in some modern series, no diagnosis may ultimately be established. However, for a standard examination question asking for the most common cause overall, infection is the accepted answer. Among the listed options, infection is therefore the best choice.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common overall cause of PUO → Infection

  • Important infection → Tuberculosis

  • Other causes → Malignancy, connective-tissue/inflammatory disorders

  • FUO may remain undiagnosed in some patients

  • Common occult infections → Abscess, endocarditis, TB

Exam Pearl: For standard exams: PUO → Infection is the most common cause.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৭) Which is not a component of Ghon's complex?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Ghon’s complex is the primary pulmonary tuberculosis lesion consisting of a Ghon focus, associated lymphangitis, and involvement of the regional hilar lymph nodes (hilar lymphadenitis). A Ghon focus is typically a small caseating lesion in the lung, often subpleural. The combination of the primary focus and regional lymph-node involvement, with lymphatic spread, forms the Ghon complex. Langhans giant cells are a histological feature of tuberculous granulomas but are not a component of Ghon’s complex itself. Therefore, among the given options, Langhans giant cell is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ghon complex → Ghon focus + lymphangitis + hilar lymphadenitis

  • Ghon focus → Primary pulmonary TB lesion

  • Langhans giant cells → Granulomatous histology

  • Ghon complex + calcification → Ranke complex

  • Primary TB commonly involves hilar lymph nodes

Exam Pearl: Ghon complex is anatomical; Langhans giant cells are histological.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৮) Which one forms apex of the heart?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The apex of the heart is formed predominantly by the left ventricle. It is directed downward, forward, and to the left and is normally located in the left 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The apex is clinically important because the apical impulse (point of maximal impulse) is normally palpated at this location. The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart, while the left atrium forms most of the posterior surface or base. The right atrium contributes mainly to the right border. Therefore, the left ventricle is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Apex → Left ventricle

  • Anterior surface → Mainly right ventricle

  • Base/posterior surface → Mainly left atrium

  • Right border → Right atrium

  • Apex beat → Left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line

Exam Pearl: Heart apex = left ventricle.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৬৯) Which one is known as spreading factor for streptococcus?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Hyaluronidase is known as the spreading factor of Streptococcus. It is an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid in the extracellular matrix, reducing the viscosity of connective tissue and facilitating the spread of bacteria through tissues. Streptococcus pyogenes produces several extracellular enzymes, including hyaluronidase, streptokinase, and DNases. Streptokinase promotes the breakdown of fibrin clots and facilitates bacterial spread through tissues, so it is also sometimes described as a spreading factor. However, in standard microbiology MCQs, hyaluronidase is classically called the spreading factor because it directly breaks down the intercellular ground substance.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hyaluronidase → Spreading factor

  • Hyaluronidase → Breaks down hyaluronic acid

  • Streptokinase → Converts plasminogen to plasmin

  • DNase → Breaks down DNA

  • Streptolysin O/S → Causes hemolysis

Exam Pearl: Hyaluronidase = spreading factor of Streptococcus.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭০) Cyanosis does not occur in ---?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Cyanosis occurs when the concentration of deoxygenated hemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds approximately 5 g/dL. In anemia, the total hemoglobin concentration is reduced, so even a significant proportion of hemoglobin may be deoxygenated without reaching the absolute concentration required to produce visible cyanosis. Therefore, cyanosis is often absent in severe anemia, despite tissue hypoxia potentially being present. In contrast, polycythemia favors cyanosis because the increased hemoglobin concentration makes the absolute amount of deoxygenated hemoglobin more likely to exceed the threshold. Hypoxia can produce cyanosis, while ITP itself does not typically cause cyanosis but is not the classic physiological answer to this question.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cyanosis → Deoxygenated Hb > ~5 g/dL

  • Anemia → Cyanosis may be absent despite hypoxia

  • Polycythemia → Cyanosis becomes more apparent

  • Central cyanosis → Tongue and mucous membranes involved

  • Peripheral cyanosis → Extremities predominantly affected

Exam Pearl: Anemia can mask cyanosis because there is insufficient total hemoglobin to reach the deoxyhemoglobin threshold.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭১) What type of hypersensitivity reaction occurs in anaphylactic shock?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Anaphylactic shock is a severe systemic manifestation of Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity. It is mediated by IgE antibodies. On first exposure, allergens induce Th2-mediated B-cell class switching and production of allergen-specific IgE, which binds to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. On subsequent exposure, allergen-mediated cross-linking of IgE triggers rapid degranulation and release of histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and other mediators. These cause vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, bronchoconstriction, and hypotension, producing anaphylactic shock. Type II and III reactions are antibody-mediated through different mechanisms, while Type IV is T-cell mediated and delayed.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:
