  • Anaphylaxis → Type I hypersensitivity

  • Main antibody → IgE

  • Key cells → Mast cells and basophils

  • Major mediator → Histamine

  • Effects → Vasodilation + increased permeability + bronchoconstriction

  • Type IV → T-cell mediated, delayed

Exam Pearl: Type I = IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity = anaphylaxis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭২) Where outlet of inguinal canal is situated?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The superficial inguinal ring is the outlet of the inguinal canal and is an opening in the aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle. It lies just above and lateral to the pubic tubercle. The deep inguinal ring, which is the entrance of the canal, is an opening in the transversalis fascia. The inguinal canal therefore extends from the deep ring to the superficial ring. The internal oblique and transversus abdominis contribute to the walls and coverings of the canal but do not form the superficial ring itself. Therefore, the external oblique aponeurosis is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Superficial inguinal ring → External oblique aponeurosis

  • Superficial ring → Outlet of inguinal canal

  • Deep inguinal ring → Transversalis fascia

  • Deep ring → Entrance of inguinal canal

  • Superficial ring lies just superolateral to pubic tubercle

Exam Pearl: Superficial ring = external oblique aponeurosis; deep ring = transversalis fascia.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৩) Which one is the most important test for recent infection with HBV?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
IgM anti-HBc is the most important serological marker of recent or acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. It appears early during acute infection and usually remains detectable for several months. Importantly, IgM anti-HBc is also the key marker that helps identify recent HBV infection during the window period, when HBsAg may have disappeared and anti-HBs has not yet appeared. IgG anti-HBc develops later and generally persists lifelong, indicating previous or ongoing infection but not specifically recent infection. Anti-HBe antibodies are associated with seroconversion from HBeAg and are not the primary marker for recent infection.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Recent/acute HBV infection → IgM anti-HBc

  • IgG anti-HBc → Past or chronic infection

  • HBsAg → Current HBV infection

  • Anti-HBs → Immunity

  • Window period → IgM anti-HBc is the key marker

Exam Pearl: IgM anti-HBc = recent/acute HBV infection and the key window-period marker.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৪) What is the expiratory reserve volume of lung?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the maximum volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a normal, quiet expiration. In a healthy adult, ERV is approximately 1100 mL. It is one of the four basic pulmonary volumes: tidal volume (about 500 mL), inspiratory reserve volume (about 3000 mL), ERV (about 1100 mL), and residual volume (about 1200 mL). ERV is reduced in conditions such as obesity and restrictive lung disease. It is important to distinguish ERV from residual volume, because residual volume cannot be voluntarily exhaled.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • ERV → ~1100 mL

  • Tidal volume → ~500 mL

  • Inspiratory reserve volume → ~3000 mL

  • Residual volume → ~1200 mL

  • ERV = Maximum additional air exhaled after normal expiration

Exam Pearl: ERV = 1100 mL; remember “extra air out after normal expiration.”

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৫) Super antigen produced by staphylococcus aureus is involved in the pathogenesis of which one of the following disease?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Staphylococcus aureus produces toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1), which acts as a superantigen. It bypasses normal antigen processing by directly cross-linking MHC class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells with T-cell receptor Vβ regions, causing massive, nonspecific T-cell activation and release of large amounts of cytokines. This produces the characteristic systemic manifestations of toxic shock syndrome, including high fever, hypotension, rash, and multiorgan involvement. In contrast, scalded skin syndrome is caused by exfoliative toxins, while impetigo is associated with localized staphylococcal infection and exfoliative toxins. Therefore, toxic shock syndrome is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • TSST-1 → Superantigen

  • TSST-1 → Toxic shock syndrome

  • Superantigen → Massive T-cell activation + cytokine release

  • Scalded skin syndrome → Exfoliative toxin A/B

  • Staphylococcal impetigo → Exfoliative toxins

Exam Pearl: S. aureus superantigen = TSST-1 = toxic shock syndrome.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৬) Abdominal aorta ends at the level of....... vertebra?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The abdominal aorta begins at the T12 vertebral level, where the thoracic aorta passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm. It descends retroperitoneally and terminates at approximately the L4 vertebral level by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries. The aortic bifurcation is an important anatomical landmark and is typically located at the level of the umbilicus. The inferior vena cava lies to the right of the abdominal aorta. Therefore, among the given options, L4 is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Abdominal aorta begins → T12

  • Abdominal aorta ends → L4

  • Termination → Right and left common iliac arteries

  • Aortic bifurcation → Approximately L4

  • Inferior vena cava → Lies to the right of the aorta

Exam Pearl: Abdominal aorta: T12 to L4.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৭) Clinical signs of decompensated CLD excludes....?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Decompensated chronic liver disease (CLD) is characterized by the development of major complications of hepatic failure and portal hypertension. Classical clinical manifestations include jaundice, ascites, hepatic encephalopathy, and variceal bleeding. Hepatomegaly is not a defining feature of decompensated CLD. In advanced cirrhosis, the liver may actually become small and shrunken because of fibrosis and loss of functional hepatic tissue. Hepatomegaly can occur in earlier liver disease or in specific causes such as fatty liver, congestive hepatopathy, or infiltrative disease, but it is not a characteristic marker of decompensation.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Decompensated CLD → Jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding

  • Advanced cirrhosis → Liver may become small and shrunken

  • Ascites → Major sign of portal hypertension

  • Encephalopathy → Indicates hepatic dysfunction

  • Hepatomegaly → Not a defining feature of decompensation

Exam Pearl: Decompensated cirrhosis classically presents with jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, or variceal bleeding—not hepatomegaly.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৮) Which nerve is involved in Hering-Breuer reflex?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The Hering–Breuer inflation reflex is mediated by the vagus nerve (CN X). Pulmonary stretch receptors located mainly in the smooth muscle of the airways are activated when the lungs become excessively inflated. Their afferent impulses travel through the vagus nerve to the respiratory centers in the medulla, where they inhibit further inspiration and promote expiration. This reflex helps prevent overdistension of the lungs, particularly during large tidal volumes. The glossopharyngeal nerve carries afferent information from the carotid body and carotid sinus, but it is not involved in the Hering–Breuer reflex.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Hering–Breuer reflex → Vagus nerve

  • Receptor → Pulmonary stretch receptor

  • Afferent pathway → CN X

  • Function → Prevents excessive lung inflation

  • Glossopharyngeal nerve → Carotid body/sinus afferents

Exam Pearl: Hering–Breuer inflation reflex = pulmonary stretch receptors → vagus → medulla.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৭৯) What is the root value of the phrenic nerve?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The phrenic nerve arises from the ventral rami of C3, C4, and C5, with the major contribution coming from C4. It is the sole motor nerve supply to the diaphragm and also provides sensory fibers to the central diaphragmatic pleura, pericardium, and peritoneum. The classic mnemonic is “C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive.” The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior surface of the anterior scalene muscle before entering the thorax. Because it originates from ventral rami, the options involving dorsal rami are incorrect.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Phrenic nerve → C3, C4, C5

  • Roots → Ventral rami

  • Major root → C4

  • Motor supply → Diaphragm

  • Mnemonic → C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive

Exam Pearl: Phrenic nerve = C3, C4, C5, mainly C4.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮০) Haldane effect is related to carriage of ___?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The Haldane effect describes how deoxygenation of hemoglobin increases its capacity to carry CO₂ and H⁺ in peripheral tissues. In tissues, hemoglobin releases O₂ and becomes deoxygenated, allowing it to bind more CO₂ as carbaminohemoglobin and buffer the H⁺ generated from CO₂ hydration. In the lungs, oxygenation of hemoglobin decreases its affinity for CO₂ and H⁺, promoting their release for exhalation. This facilitates efficient CO₂ transport from tissues to the lungs. The Haldane effect therefore complements the Bohr effect, which concerns the effect of CO₂/H⁺ on oxygen unloading.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Haldane effect → CO₂ transport

  • Deoxygenated Hb → Increased CO₂ carrying capacity

  • Oxygenation in lungs → CO₂ unloading

  • Bohr effect → CO₂/H⁺ promotes O₂ unloading

  • CO₂ transported mainly as bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻)

Exam Pearl: Haldane = deoxygenated Hb carries more CO₂.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮১) What is the type of aortic opening?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The aortic opening (aortic hiatus) of the diaphragm is a tendinous opening. It is located at the T12 vertebral level and lies posterior to the median arcuate ligament. The aorta, thoracic duct, and often the azygos vein pass through it. Unlike the esophageal hiatus, which is primarily muscular and located at T10, the aortic hiatus is formed between the crura of the diaphragm and the median arcuate ligament, making it tendinous and relatively unaffected by diaphragmatic contraction. This anatomical arrangement prevents significant compression of the aorta during inspiration.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Aortic hiatus → T12

  • Type → Tendinous

  • Contents → Aorta + thoracic duct + azygos vein

  • Esophageal hiatus → T10

  • Caval opening → T8

  • Mnemonic → “I 8, 10 Eggs, At 12”

Exam Pearl: Aortic hiatus = tendinous, T12.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮২) Which of the following factor does not prevent collapsing tendency of lung?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The lung has an inherent tendency to collapse inward because of its elastic recoil and surface tension. Several factors oppose this collapsing tendency. Pulmonary surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, thereby preventing alveolar collapse. Negative intrapleural pressure keeps the lungs expanded by creating a transpulmonary pressure gradient. Residual volume also helps maintain alveolar patency and prevents complete lung collapse after expiration. In contrast, positive intrapleural pressure would reduce or reverse the normal transpulmonary pressure gradient and therefore does not prevent lung collapse. It may contribute to lung compression, as occurs with tension pneumothorax.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Surfactant → ↓ Surface tension

  • Negative intrapleural pressure → Keeps lung expanded

  • Residual volume → Prevents complete lung collapse

  • Positive intrapleural pressure → Promotes lung compression/collapse

Exam Pearl: Negative intrapleural pressure keeps the lung expanded; positive intrapleural pressure does the opposite.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৩) What is the location of gastric gland?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Gastric glands are located in the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa. They extend downward from the gastric pits and contain different cell types, including parietal cells, chief cells, mucous neck cells, and enteroendocrine cells. The stomach wall follows the typical GI tract arrangement: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, and serosa. The lamina propria is the connective tissue layer within the mucosa that contains the gastric glands. The submucosa contains larger blood vessels, lymphatics, and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus but does not contain the gastric glands.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Gastric glands → Lamina propria

  • Gastric pits → Invaginations of surface epithelium

  • Parietal cells → HCl + intrinsic factor

  • Chief cells → Pepsinogen

  • Submucosa → Larger vessels + Meissner plexus

Exam Pearl: Gastric glands are present in the lamina propria of the gastric mucosa.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৪) Enteropeptidase is a proteolytic enzyme which is a component of…?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Enteropeptidase (enterokinase) is a proteolytic enzyme located on the brush border of duodenal enterocytes, making it a component of succus entericus (intestinal juice). Its main function is to convert trypsinogen into active trypsin. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens, including chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, and procarboxypeptidases. Enteropeptidase itself is therefore crucial for initiating the activation cascade of pancreatic digestive enzymes. It is not a component of saliva, gastric juice, or pancreatic juice.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Enteropeptidase → Succus entericus

  • Location → Duodenal brush border

  • Converts → Trypsinogen → Trypsin

  • Trypsin activates → Other pancreatic zymogens

  • Also called → Enterokinase

Exam Pearl: Enteropeptidase is a brush-border enzyme of the duodenum → succus entericus.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৫) What is the main artery of stomach?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The left gastric artery is considered the main artery of the stomach. It is the smallest branch of the celiac trunk and supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach. It also gives esophageal branches that supply the lower esophagus. The stomach receives additional arterial supply from the right gastric artery, left and right gastroepiploic arteries, and short gastric arteries. Among the given options, the left gastric artery is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Main artery of stomach → Left gastric artery

  • Origin → Celiac trunk

  • Runs along → Lesser curvature

  • Greater curvature → Right & left gastroepiploic arteries

  • Fundus → Short gastric arteries

Exam Pearl: Left gastric = main artery of stomach + branch of celiac trunk.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৬) Which is not true about ecbolic secretion?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Ecbolic secretion refers to the enzyme-rich secretion of the pancreas, particularly stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK). CCK is released from I cells of the duodenum and jejunum mainly in response to fatty acids and amino acids. Therefore, fatty food strongly stimulates ecbolic pancreatic secretion. In contrast, secretin primarily stimulates the pancreas to produce a hydro (bicarbonate-rich, watery) secretion, rather than the enzyme-rich ecbolic secretion. Hence, “stimulated by secretin” is the statement that is not true.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Ecbolic secretion → Enzyme-rich pancreatic secretion

  • Main stimulus → CCK

  • Fatty food → Strongly stimulates CCK

  • Secretin → Stimulates bicarbonate-rich hydro secretion

  • CCK → Pancreatic enzyme secretion

Exam Pearl: CCK → Ecbolic (enzyme-rich); Secretin → Hydro (bicarbonate-rich).

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৭) What is the most common position of appendix?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The retrocecal position is the most common position of the vermiform appendix, accounting for roughly 60–65% of cases. In this position, the appendix lies behind the cecum and may extend upward toward the right flank. Other positions include pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, and post-ileal. The position is clinically important because a retrocecal appendix may produce less prominent classical right lower-quadrant tenderness and can sometimes cause flank or back pain. The appendix is attached to the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, and its base is located at the convergence of the three taeniae coli.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common appendix position → Retrocecal

  • Frequency → Approximately 60–65%

  • Base → Convergence of 3 taeniae coli

  • Other positions → Pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, post-ileal

  • Retrocecal appendicitis → May cause flank/back pain

Exam Pearl: Retrocecal = most common position of appendix.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৮) Which is a typical features of cortical nephron?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Cortical nephrons constitute approximately 85% of all nephrons and are located mainly in the outer cortex. They have relatively short loops of Henle that extend only a short distance into the medulla. Their primary role is routine urine formation, including filtration, reabsorption, and secretion. In contrast, juxtamedullary nephrons account for about 15% of nephrons, are located near the corticomedullary junction, and possess long loops of Henle that extend deep into the medulla. These juxtamedullary nephrons are particularly important for producing concentrated urine.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Cortical nephrons → ~85%

  • Location → Outer cortex

  • Loop of Henle → Short

  • Juxtamedullary nephrons → ~15%

  • Juxtamedullary loop → Long

  • Both types → Participate in urine formation

Exam Pearl: Cortical nephron = 85%, outer cortex, short loop of Henle.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৮৯) What is the most common site of carcinoma in large gut?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The rectum is classically considered the most common site of carcinoma in the large intestine in standard anatomy/pathology MCQs. Colorectal carcinoma commonly occurs in the rectosigmoid region, with the rectum being a frequent individual site. The sigmoid colon is another common location, while the caecum and transverse colon are less common compared with the distal large bowel. Therefore, among the given options, rectum is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Most common site of large bowel carcinoma → Rectum

  • Rectum + sigmoid → Rectosigmoid region is commonly involved

  • Caecum → More associated with right-sided lesions

  • Left-sided lesions → More likely to cause altered bowel habit/obstruction

Exam Pearl: Large gut carcinoma → Rectum is the classic MCQ answer.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯০) Water turnover in adult is..?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Water turnover in an adult is approximately 20% of total body water per day. In a healthy adult, daily water loss occurs mainly through urine, with additional losses through the skin, lungs, and feces. Water intake from drinking and food replaces these losses, maintaining fluid balance. A typical adult may turn over around 2–2.5 L of water daily, depending on environmental conditions, physical activity, and diet. In infants, water turnover is proportionally higher because of their greater metabolic rate and higher extracellular fluid turnover.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Adult water turnover → ~20% of total body water/day

  • Daily water turnover → Approximately 2–2.5 L/day

  • Major route of loss → Urine

  • Other losses → Skin + lungs + feces

  • Infants → Higher water turnover

Exam Pearl: Adult water turnover ≈ 20% of total body water per day.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯১) Which vein drain into portal system?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The superior rectal vein drains into the inferior mesenteric vein, which ultimately joins the portal venous system. In contrast, the middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac vein and then the systemic venous circulation. This arrangement creates an important portosystemic anastomosis around the rectum. The superior rectal vein represents the portal side, while the middle and inferior rectal veins represent the systemic side. The middle sacral vein drains into the common iliac vein or inferior vena cava and is not part of the portal system.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Superior rectal vein → Portal system

  • Superior rectal → Inferior mesenteric vein

  • Middle rectal → Internal iliac vein → systemic

  • Inferior rectal → Internal pudendal → internal iliac → systemic

  • Rectal portosystemic anastomosis → Superior ↔ middle/inferior rectal veins

Exam Pearl: Superior rectal = portal; middle & inferior rectal = systemic.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯২) Which type of dwarfism occurs due to deficiency of somatomedin?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Somatomedin (IGF-1) deficiency causes Laron/Levi-Lorain dwarfism, which results from growth hormone (GH) resistance rather than lack of GH itself. In this condition, GH secretion is normal or increased, but the tissues cannot respond properly because of a defect in the GH receptor, leading to reduced hepatic production of IGF-1 (somatomedin C). Consequently, linear growth is severely impaired. In contrast, GH deficiency dwarfism is caused by inadequate secretion of GH, while panhypopituitarism involves deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Somatomedin/IGF-1 deficiency → Laron (Levi-Lorain) dwarfism

  • Laron syndrome → GH receptor resistance

  • GH level → Normal/high

  • IGF-1 level → Low

  • GH deficiency dwarfism → Low GH + low IGF-1

Exam Pearl: Laron dwarfism = GH resistance → ↓ somatomedin (IGF-1).

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৩) Which is the main support of liver?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
The hepatic veins are considered an important main support of the liver, as they anchor the liver to the inferior vena cava and posterior abdominal wall. The liver is also supported by its peritoneal ligaments, especially the falciform and coronary ligaments, but these are not the principal mechanical support. The hepatic veins pass from the liver directly into the inferior vena cava, helping maintain the liver's position. Therefore, among the given options, hepatic vein is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Main support of liver → Hepatic veins

  • Hepatic veins → Drain into IVC

  • Falciform ligament → Divides anatomical right and left lobes

  • Coronary ligament → Helps attach liver to diaphragm

  • Liver is largely intraperitoneal except for the bare area

Exam Pearl: Hepatic veins are the major posterior anchoring support of the liver.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৪) Which joint is involved in inversion eversion movement?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Inversion and eversion of the foot occur mainly at the subtalar (talocalcaneal) joint, with contribution from the talocalcaneonavicular joint. Inversion turns the sole of the foot medially, while eversion turns it laterally. The ankle (talocrural) joint primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, not inversion/eversion. The knee is mainly responsible for flexion and extension, with limited rotation when flexed. Therefore, among the given options, the subtalar joint is the correct answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Inversion/eversion → Subtalar joint

  • Inversion → Sole faces medially

  • Eversion → Sole faces laterally

  • Ankle joint → Dorsiflexion + plantarflexion

  • Subtalar joint → Talocalcaneal joint

Exam Pearl: Inversion + eversion = subtalar joint.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৫) Urine formation occurs in following steps excludes..?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Urine formation occurs through three main processes: glomerular filtration, tubular reabsorption, and tubular secretion. Glomerular filtration occurs at the renal corpuscle, where plasma is filtered from the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule. Tubular reabsorption returns useful substances such as water, glucose, and electrolytes from the tubular fluid back into the blood. Tubular secretion transfers substances from the blood into the tubular fluid. “Tubular filtration” is not a recognized step of urine formation; filtration occurs specifically at the glomerulus.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Urine formation → 3 processes

    • Glomerular filtration

    • Tubular reabsorption

    • Tubular secretion

  • Glomerular filtration → Glomerulus → Bowman's capsule

  • Tubular reabsorption → Tubule → Blood

  • Tubular secretion → Blood → Tubule

  • Tubular filtration → Not a standard process

Exam Pearl: GFR + tubular reabsorption + tubular secretion = urine formation.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৬) Rothera’s test is positive in which of the following condition??
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Rothera’s test is a qualitative test for detecting ketone bodies in urine, particularly acetoacetate and acetone. It is therefore positive in conditions associated with significant ketosis, especially diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In DKA, insulin deficiency leads to increased lipolysis and hepatic ketone-body production, resulting in ketonemia and ketonuria. Rothera’s test uses sodium nitroprusside, which reacts with acetoacetate and acetone to produce a characteristic purple color. It does not detect β-hydroxybutyrate effectively. The other options—diabetic retinopathy, diabetes insipidus, and diabetic nephropathy—do not characteristically cause ketonuria.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Rothera’s test → Urinary ketone bodies

  • Positive in → DKA

  • Detects → Acetoacetate + acetone

  • Reagent → Sodium nitroprusside

  • Does not reliably detect → β-hydroxybutyrate

Exam Pearl: Rothera positive = ketonuria → think diabetic ketoacidosis.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৭) Heat stroke occurs above which temperature (degree C)?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Heat stroke is a medical emergency characterized by severe hyperthermia, classically with a core body temperature ≥40°C (104°F) along with central nervous system dysfunction such as confusion, altered consciousness, seizures, or coma. It results from failure of the body's thermoregulatory mechanisms. Heat stroke may be classic (non-exertional) or exertional. Sweating may be present or absent, so absence of sweating is not required for diagnosis. Among the given options, 40°C is the standard examination answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Heat stroke → Core temperature ≥40°C

  • Key feature → CNS dysfunction

  • Types → Classic + exertional

  • Sweating → May be present or absent

  • Heat exhaustion → Usually <40°C, without major CNS dysfunction

Exam Pearl: Core temperature ≥40°C + CNS dysfunction = heat stroke.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৮) What type of fever occurs in kala-azar?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
In kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis), the fever is classically irregular or remittent, with fluctuations in temperature but without returning to normal between episodes. The fever may be prolonged and associated with massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, pancytopenia, and weight loss. Tertian and quartan fevers are classically associated with malaria, while double quotidian fever can occur in conditions such as certain bacterial infections and adult Still disease. Therefore, among the given options, remittent fever is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Kala-azar → Remittent/irregular fever

  • Cause → Leishmania donovani

  • Major features → Fever + massive splenomegaly + pancytopenia

  • Tertian fever → Classically P. vivax / P. falciparum

  • Quartan fever → P. malariae

Exam Pearl: Kala-azar → prolonged irregular/remittent fever + massive splenomegaly.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ৯৯) Air bronchogram in CXR mostly signifies......?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
An air bronchogram on chest X-ray occurs when air-filled bronchi become visible against surrounding opacified lung tissue. This is most commonly seen in lung consolidation, particularly in pneumonia. Normally, bronchi are not visible because both the bronchi and surrounding alveoli contain air. When alveoli become filled with fluid, pus, blood, or cells while the bronchi remain air-filled, the bronchi appear as dark branching structures within the white area of consolidation. Air bronchograms can also occur in pulmonary edema and other alveolar-filling conditions, but among the given options, consolidation is the best answer.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Air bronchogram → Consolidation

  • Bronchi → Air-filled

  • Alveoli → Fluid/pus-filled

  • Common cause → Pneumonia

  • Usually indicates an alveolar air-space process

Exam Pearl: Air bronchogram = air-filled bronchi surrounded by consolidated lung.

Health Part (100 Marks).question: ১০০) To Select General Part, please click on 'Health Part (100 Marks)' Topic Name option. Saw tooth appearance of P waves are found in ECG of..........?
Health Part (100 Marks).exp:
Saw-tooth (F) waves on ECG are characteristic of atrial flutter. They result from rapid, regular atrial depolarization, typically at an atrial rate of around 250–350 beats/minute. The flutter waves are best seen in the inferior leads (II, III, aVF). Atrial flutter commonly shows 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 AV conduction, producing a ventricular rate that is often around 150/min with 2:1 conduction. In atrial fibrillation, the atrial activity is chaotic and produces fibrillatory (f) waves rather than organized saw-tooth waves.

High-Yield Rapid Recall:

  • Saw-tooth F waves → Atrial flutter

  • Atrial flutter rate → ~250–350/min

  • Best seen → II, III, aVF

  • Common conduction → 2:1 AV block

  • Atrial fibrillation → Irregularly irregular rhythm + absent organized P waves

Exam Pearl: Saw-tooth P/F waves = atrial flutter.
